name: Ukrainian SSR
info: The Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic was a constituent republic of the Soviet Union, ruled by the Communist Party of Ukraine, remembered for the Holodomor, the devastation of the Second World War and its declaration of independence in 1991.

facts.founder: The Bolsheviks; the Third All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets ratified its constitution in Kharkiv on 10 March 1919
facts.predecessor: The Ukrainian People's Republic of Soviets and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic, against the Ukrainian People's Republic

t: On 30 December 1922 the Ukrainian SSR became one of the four founding republics of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
The famine of 1932–1933 known as the Holodomor, caused by Stalin's regime's agricultural policies, cost an estimated 2.6 million to 10 million lives; whether it was genocide is disputed.
On 24 August 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, and on 1 December 92.3% of voters voted for independence.
dyk: Although it was part of the Soviet Union, the Ukrainian SSR was a founding member of the United Nations in 1945 and an elected member of the Security Council in 1948–1949 and 1984–1985.
ev: The Third All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets ratified the Constitution of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in Kharkiv
The Ukrainian SSR joined the Russian, Byelorussian and Transcaucasian republics in founding the USSR
The Holodomor famine killed millions after forced collectivisation and grain requisitions
After the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Eastern Galicia, Volhynia, Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina were attached to the republic
Nazi Germany occupied all of Soviet Ukraine and murdered about 1,554,000 Jews within Ukraine's present borders
The Ukrainian SSR became a founding member of the United Nations, and Carpathian Ruthenia was transferred to it
The Chernobyl disaster turned many Ukrainians against Soviet rule
The Supreme Soviet adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, ending the Ukrainian SSR

sections.foundation:
After the Russian Revolution of 1917 several factions sought an independent Ukrainian state. The internationally recognised Ukrainian People's Republic in Kiev faced a Soviet Russia-aligned government in Kharkov. The Bolsheviks declared the first Soviet Republic of Ukraine on 24 December 1917, beginning the Ukrainian–Soviet War, part of both the Russian Civil War and the Ukrainian War of Independence. That republic was dissolved after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, when the Bolsheviks were forced out of Ukraine.

In July 1918 the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of Ukraine was founded in Moscow, and after the Central Powers' defeat a Provisional Workers' and Peasants' Government was set up at Kursk in November 1918. On 10 March 1919 the Third All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets ratified the constitution of the Ukrainian Socialist Soviet Republic in Kharkiv. Requisitioners from Russia met resistance, and from mid-1919 the republic's defence, economy, finance and transport were subordinated to Russia's commissariats; some historians hold that Soviet Ukraine was under Soviet Russia's control from then. After the Peace of Riga the Red Army held most of Ukraine, western Ukraine going to Poland. On 30 December 1922 the republic became a founding member of the USSR, its name changed to Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936–1937.
sections.socioeconomy:
At the start more than 90% of the workforce were peasants. War Communism and food requisitions devastated the economy: by early 1921 only 4,060 of more than 10,000 industrial enterprises still worked, and a famine of 1921–1923 claimed up to one million lives. The New Economic Policy brought recovery, until from 1925 the regime turned to industrialisation and collectivisation. In the Holodomor of 1932–1933, while Moscow exported over a million tonnes of grain, the famine caused a direct loss of life estimated at between 2.6 million and 10 million. Between 1928 and 1937 the republic's industry grew at record rates; it became Europe's second biggest producer of pig iron and fourth in the world in coal.

After the war, the Fourth Five-Year Plan restored industry: by 1955 Ukraine was producing 2.2 times more than in 1940, the largest per-capita producer in Europe of pig iron and sugar. Agriculture lagged, and growth slowed to 3.5% in the Eleventh Five-Year Plan (1981–1985). Dnieper reservoirs, natural gas and a nuclear programme supplied energy. Peasants' private plots grew more than half of all potatoes. The population reached 51,706,746 in 1989, and by 1979 53% of ethnic Ukrainians lived in towns; Kiev grew from 1.1 million in 1959 to 2.1 million in 1979.
sections.military:
The republic's defence was managed by the Soviet Armed Forces; a 1944 clause allowing it a standing army of its own was never fulfilled. Its land was the theatre of some of the largest battles of the German-Soviet War from June 1941. Soviet armies were defeated at the Battle of Brody, over 100,000 Red Army soldiers were encircled at Uman, and in the ring east of Kyiv 453,000 Soviet soldiers and officers were captured, by Soviet data; Kyiv was abandoned on 18 September 1941. A failed counteroffensive near Kharkiv in 1942 cost 171,000 dead and 240,000 captured, and by 27 July 1942 all of Soviet Ukraine was occupied. The retreating Soviet forces evacuated over 550 enterprises and destroyed what they could not move, including the Dnieper Hydroelectric Station.

Soviet partisans under Tymofiy Strokach and nationalist guerrillas of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) both fought the occupiers; in July 1943 UPA forces under Dmytro Klyachkivsky carried out ethnic cleansing of Poles in Volhynia. Soviet armies entered Kyiv on 6 November 1943 and expelled German troops from Transcarpathia by 28 October 1944. The NKVD then fought the UPA, killing over 103,000 rebels in 1944–1945; its commander Roman Shukhevych was killed in 1950, and the insurgency faded after 1954.
sections.governance:
The Ukrainian SSR was governed by the Communist Party of Ukraine, the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union; real power lay with the party's politburo and First Secretary, and the regime can be characterised as a form of party oligarchy. Legislative authority lay first with the Congress of Soviets, whose Central Executive Committee was long headed by Grigory Petrovsky, and then with a Supreme Soviet of 450 deputies, which met only a few weeks a year; elections every five years were symbolic. The republic was divided into oblasts, 25 by 1991, and 490 raions, with Kiev and Sevastopol as cities with special status.

The secret police, the Cheka and its successor the GPU, acted as a "state within a state", staging annual show trials. In the 1920s korenizatsiya took the form of Ukrainization, halted in 1932–1933. Stalinist terror struck National Communists, specialists and the intelligentsia; Mykola Skrypnyk and Mykola Khvylyovy were driven to suicide, and hundreds of thousands were executed. After Stalin, Aleksey Kirichenko became in 1953 the first ethnic Ukrainian to lead the party since the 1920s; Petro Shelest, removed in 1972, was followed by Volodymyr Shcherbytsky's Russification.
sections.impact:
The republic's borders changed many times. Under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact it gained Eastern Galicia and Volhynia from Poland in 1939 and lands of Romania in 1940, reaching 560,000 sq km; in 1945 it gained Carpathian Ruthenia from Czechoslovakia. Population exchanges moved 810,400 Poles to Poland and 482,900 Ukrainians from it between 1944 and 1946. In 1954 the Russian SFSR transferred Crimea to Ukraine. In the 1920s it had ceded Belgorod, Taganrog and Starodub to Russia.

The republic also had a place in the world. In the early 1920s it signed treaties with Estonia and Latvia and had its own diplomats until 1923. From 1945 it sat in the United Nations as a founding member, giving the Soviet Union two extra votes in the General Assembly, and joined bodies from UNESCO to the International Atomic Energy Agency. Its culture lived under repression: more than half the members of the Writers' Union were repressed between 1934 and 1938, churches fell from about 10,000 to 850 by 1937, and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church was abolished in 1946. Yet Kyiv gave the world Alexander Dovzhenko's Arsenal and Earth and the poetic cinema of Sergei Parajanov, and dissidents such as Ivan Dziuba, Viacheslav Chornovil and the Ukrainian Helsinki Group of 1976 kept up opposition.
sections.decline:
Perestroika reached Ukraine late under the conservative Shcherbytsky, but the Chernobyl disaster of 1986, Russification and stagnation turned many against Soviet rule. Glasnost brought the Holodomor into the open. Civic groups grew: the Ukrainian Helsinki Union under Levko Lukianenko in 1988, the People's Movement of Ukraine (Rukh) in September 1989, which by October 1990 had 633,000 activists. In October 1989 the Law on Languages made Ukrainian the state language. On 21 January 1990 hundreds of thousands formed a human chain from Kyiv to Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk.

On 16 July 1990 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty, and Leonid Kravchuk became its head. A students' hunger strike in October 1990 forced out the prime minister Vitaliy Masol. When the August Coup began in Moscow on 19 August 1991, Kravchuk hesitated, then defended sovereignty; on 24 August the Supreme Soviet adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, ending the Ukrainian SSR, and the Communist Party of Ukraine was banned days later. On 1 December 1991 92.3% voted for independence and Kravchuk was elected president with 62 percent. On 8 December he signed the Belovezh Accords, and the Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991. Ukraine became its legal successor and kept its UN seat.

summary: The Ukrainian SSR was the Soviet Union's second republic in population and economic power, created by the Bolsheviks against the Ukrainian People's Republic and governed from Kharkov, then Kiev. It suffered the Holodomor, the Stalinist terror and the German occupation, grew into an industrial heartland, and ended in 1991 when its Supreme Soviet declared Ukraine independent.

pointDescs.1919: The Third All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets ratified the republic's constitution in Kharkiv amid civil war.
pointDescs.1921: War Communism had left only 4,060 of more than 10,000 enterprises working, and famine struck Southern Ukraine.
pointDescs.1922: The Ukrainian SSR became a founding republic of the USSR on 30 December.
pointDescs.1928: The turn to industrialisation began a decade of record industrial growth, to 1937.
pointDescs.1933: The Holodomor famine caused millions of deaths after forced collectivisation and requisitions.
pointDescs.1937: Industry had grown rapidly, though the terror was at its height and fewer than half the population still worked in agriculture by the late 1930s.
pointDescs.1940: With western lands annexed after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the republic reached 560,000 sq km and 41,657,000 people.
pointDescs.1942: By 27 July all of Soviet Ukraine was under German occupation.
pointDescs.1944: Soviet armies drove the Germans out, the last from Transcarpathia by 28 October.
pointDescs.1945: The republic became a founding member of the United Nations and gained Carpathian Ruthenia.
pointDescs.1955: Industrial output was 2.2 times that of 1940; Crimea had been transferred to Ukraine in 1954.
pointDescs.1965: Industrial growth began to slow after the post-war boom, under Brezhnev's new leadership.
pointDescs.1979: Kiev had 2.1 million people and the majority of ethnic Ukrainians lived in towns.
pointDescs.1986: The Chernobyl disaster deepened opposition to Soviet rule.
pointDescs.1990: The Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty on 16 July.
pointDescs.1991: The Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine on 24 August ended the Ukrainian SSR.

notes: The article's reference lists were not saved; the only source line is a web article by Stephen Velychenko (not a book), so references are empty.
Holodomor: the death range (2.6 to 10 million) and the genocide debate are kept as the article gives them; the economy section's 'four million' figure was left out to avoid two different numbers.
The power curve is my reading (population, industry, sovereignty) of a constituent republic; peak 1979 is a judgement, not an article statement of a peak.
